title: Central bank digital currencies, financial subordination and the quest for infrastructural autonomy: the introduction of the eNaira in Nigeria
summary: Political economists have only recently begun to grapple with the question of how to conceptualise and systematically explain the responses of states in lower-income countries to the rise of digital money. This article connects scholarship on financial infrastructures and international financial subordination to conceptualise the factors that explain the investments of central banks in lower-income countries in the development of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs). My main contention is that limited control of infrastructure is an important dimension of international financial subordination. I illustrate this argument focusing on the case of Nigeria, the second country in the world which launched a CBDC. My analysis suggests that Nigeria introduced her CBDC, the eNaira, to enhance her autonomy in the context of a subordinated position in the global financial and monetary system. Nigerian authorities considered the eNaira as a state-controlled financial infrastructure which they envisaged to reduce the reliance on externally controlled payment infrastructures. As such, this paper contributes to broader debates about how lower-income countries navigate the disruptions associated with FinTech. This includes the questions of how much sovereignty they have in the governance of digital financial infrastructures and how much influence foreign players have over their digital financial infrastructure.

title: Assessing Students' Conceptual Understanding of an Islamic Financial System Course Using the Rasch Wright Map
summary: The rapid growth of Islamic finance has increased the need for effective assessment methods that accurately evaluate students’ conceptual understanding of Islamic financial principles beyond the traditional score-based approaches. title: Offshore Financial Centres and Banks' Funding Responses to Liquidity Shocks
summary: This paper rethinks financial embeddedness by examining how transnational banks respond to funding pressures through the infrastructures of offshore financial centres (OFCs). Using handcollected information, we construct a novel dataset of European banks across six Eurozone countries from 2009 to 2015. We show that during the sovereign debt crisis, banks engaged in latent network activation, mobilising offshore conduit arrangements to secure foreign currency funding as market conditions tightened, even when official liquidity support was available. We argue that embeddedness in global finance is dynamic and crisis contingent, since relationships and organisational infrastructures that appear peripheral in stable periods can become decisive under stress. OFCs emerge not as passive enablers of regulatory arbitrage, but as active infrastructures used by global banks to access cross-border liquidity when conventional funding channels become impaired. This has important implications for the governance and oversight of cross-border liquidity flows and off-balance-sheet funding structures.
